clinicalPearls: A highly aggressive germinal-centre B-cell lymphoma defined by MYC translocation, most often t(8;14) juxtaposing MYC with the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus

Recognised in three clinical settings: endemic (equatorial Africa, strongly Epstein-Barr virus associated, often jaw and facial bones), sporadic (worldwide, often abdominal), and immunodeficiency-associated (notably HIV)
Histology shows a monotonous sheet of medium-sized cells with a very high proliferation fraction and a starry-sky appearance from interspersed tingible-body macrophages
The immunophenotype is CD20-positive, CD10-positive and BCL6-positive with BCL2 typically negative or weak and a Ki-67 proliferation index approaching 100 per cent
It is one of the fastest-growing human tumours, so it is a haematological emergency with a high risk of tumour lysis syndrome at presentation and with treatment
Curable with intensive, short-duration multi-agent chemoimmunotherapy including central nervous system prophylaxis and anti-CD20 targeted therapy

A single MYC rearrangement in the appropriate morphological and immunophenotypic context supports the diagnosis, distinguishing it from high-grade B-cell lymphomas with additional BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangements
reference.pathophysiology: Burkitt lymphoma arises from a germinal-centre B cell and is driven by translocation of the MYC oncogene, usually to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus, causing constitutive MYC overexpression that powerfully drives proliferation and metabolic reprogramming. In endemic disease Epstein-Barr virus infection and chronic immune stimulation, including from malaria, contribute to lymphomagenesis, whereas immunodeficiency-associated cases relate to impaired immune surveillance in HIV infection. Cooperating mutations, for example in TCF3 and ID3, sustain tonic B-cell receptor and PI3K signalling. The resulting extremely high proliferative rate produces the characteristic starry-sky histology and the marked propensity for rapid tumour growth and tumour lysis.
additionalDifferentials: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements (double/triple hit)
Acute leukaemia with mature B-cell phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Urgent biopsy with immunohistochemistry showing CD20, CD10, BCL6 positivity and near-100 per cent Ki-67
FISH for MYC rearrangement and assessment for concurrent BCL2/BCL6 rearrangements to exclude double-hit lymphoma
Baseline tumour lysis markers including urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium and renal function
Lactate dehydrogenase and full blood count
Bone marrow and cerebrospinal fluid examination for staging and central nervous system involvement
HIV testing and Epstein-Barr virus assessment where relevant
redFlags: Tumour lysis syndrome with hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperphosphataemia and acute kidney injury
Rapidly enlarging bulky abdominal or facial mass causing obstruction or compression
Central nervous system involvement with neurological deficit
Spontaneous tumour lysis before treatment begins
reference.prognosis: Despite its aggressiveness Burkitt lymphoma is highly curable with intensive short-course chemoimmunotherapy and central nervous system prophylaxis, particularly in children and in limited-stage disease; prognosis is worse with advanced age, bulky or central nervous system disease, and delays in initiating treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to anticipate and prevent tumour lysis syndrome, which can be fatal
Delaying treatment of a rapidly growing tumour while awaiting complete staging
Misclassifying a double-hit high-grade lymphoma as Burkitt lymphoma by not testing for BCL2/BCL6 rearrangements
Omitting central nervous system prophylaxis given the high risk of central nervous system disease
Using a standard-intensity diffuse large B-cell regimen, which is inadequate for cure
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on Burkitt lymphoma
